ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT in Charleston, SC
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Charleston, SC: thickness surveys and weld examination on tanks, piping, vessels and port steel, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Charleston, South Carolina
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Charleston, South Carolina: thickness surveys on corroding steel, and angle-beam examination of welds on pressure equipment, piping, tanks and structural steel around the harbor and the Cooper River. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope and report readings against the locations and criteria you specify. Send the equipment list through the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used in Charleston

Charleston is a port-and-manufacturing economy, and ultrasonic testing follows the steel. The harbor is dredged to 52 feet, the container terminals run ship-to-shore cranes, and the former Navy base area on the Cooper River has been redeveloped for port use. Behind the docks sit rail spurs, bulk and liquid storage, a kraft paper mill on the river, aircraft assembly in North Charleston and a long list of plants making engines, vans and turbochargers. Each of them owns steel that thins, cracks or gets repaired.

  • Storage tanks and process piping: bottom plates, shell courses, nozzles and the piping that feeds fuel, chemical and food-grade tanks near the port.
  • Pressure equipment in process and power service: steam piping, boiler and recovery equipment, air receivers and heat exchangers, including the high-pressure systems a paper mill depends on.
  • Marine and dockside steel: crane girders, boom sections, spreader bars, bollard foundations and the repair welds that come with heavy cycling loads.
  • Structural and bridge steel: connection plates, gusset welds and bracing on buildings, rail structures and highway steel.

Salt air, humid summers and brackish water make external corrosion under insulation and coating failure a routine finding in Charleston, which is why thickness mapping appears in so many inspection plans here.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends high-frequency sound into the material and times the echoes that return. For thickness work the echo from the back wall gives remaining wall; for weld work the echo from a flaw gives its position and an amplitude to size against a reference. That makes UT the main tool for internal conditions such as general wall loss, pitting, lamination, lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and slag that a surface method cannot see.

The limits matter just as much. Rough, scaled or heavily pitted surfaces scatter the beam and reduce accuracy, so surface preparation is part of the job. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic welds attenuate sound and need a qualified technique. Very thin sections and curved surfaces need the right probe and a calibration block of similar geometry. Planar flaws oriented parallel to the beam can be missed, which is why weld examination uses angle beams from more than one direction. A good report states these limits instead of hiding them.

Charleston's coastal environment adds one more consideration: pitting under failed coating and under insulation is common, and a thickness grid can miss a pit that is smaller than the probe face. Where pitting is expected, the plan should call for closer grid spacing or scanning the suspect area rather than relying on a single reading per location.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern the work

The acceptance criteria belong to the construction or in-service code, not to the inspection company. For process piping, ASME B31.3 sets the examination method and the acceptance table. Vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use its Mandatory Appendix 12 when welds are examined ultrasonically. Structural groove welds under AWS D1.1 carry their own UT acceptance classes, and steel highway bridges follow AWS D1.5. Method requirements sit in ASME Section V: Article 4 for weld examination and Article 5 for materials, with thickness measurement practices in SE-797 inside Article 23. ASTM E797 is the standard practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and ASTM E164 covers contact examination of weldments.

For equipment already in service, the owner's inspection program follows API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. Under those codes the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Atlantis provides the ultrasonic data, such as thickness at condition monitoring locations, and the inspector makes the fitness and interval decisions. OSHA's process safety rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), expects mechanical integrity inspections to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and thickness records are among the first documents an auditor asks for.

South Carolina adds its own layer for boilers and pressure vessels. The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act (Title 41, Chapter 14 of the state code) is administered through the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, which recognizes ASME and National Board stamps and issues special inspector certificates. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, so a weld found defective by UT usually leads to a repair procedure that has to satisfy it.

Technique: how a thickness survey and a weld scan are performed

A thickness survey starts with a grid or a list of condition monitoring locations marked on the isometric or drawing. The technician cleans each spot to bright metal where needed, applies couplant and takes readings with a dual-element probe, which handles corroded and pitted surfaces better than a single-element probe. The instrument is calibrated on a step block made of the same material before work starts and checked again during and after. An A-scan display is used where the wall is thin or pitted, because a thickness gauge alone can lock onto a double echo or a lamination and report a number that looks plausible and is wrong. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant, and the reading is corrected for temperature.

Weld examination uses an angle-beam probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, on a wedge. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a block of the same material and thickness range, scanning gain is set above the reference, and the weld is scanned from both sides with the beam skewed to cover the fusion faces and root. Every indication is evaluated for position, length and amplitude, then compared with the acceptance table in the code that governs the weld.

Scope and re-inspection planning

Agree the number and placement of measurement locations before the crew travels. In-service programs rank locations by risk: injection points, dead legs, bends, and anywhere past surveys showed loss. Repeating readings at the same marked spots at later intervals is what turns a single survey into a corrosion rate. For construction welds, the scope usually follows a percentage set by the code, and a rejected weld normally widens the sample.

Who performs the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified and certified by the company under its written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Under that scheme a Level II technician sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results, while an ASNT NDT Level III writes and approves the procedures and reviews reports. Procedures for Charleston jobs are written to the governing code and revision, and the Level III review is what turns a pile of readings into a record that survives an audit. If your own procedure or written practice needs work, the Level III consulting service and written practice development pages describe what is available.

What the ultrasonic report contains

  • Component identification, drawing or isometric reference, and the exact locations examined.
  • The procedure number and revision, the governing code and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probe, wedge, couplant and calibration block, with calibration checks recorded before and after.
  • For thickness work: a reading at every location, the nominal and minimum required wall where supplied, and a grid or table that shows the thinnest point.
  • For welds: each indication with location, length, amplitude against the reference and an accept or reject call, plus a sketch showing where it sits in the joint.
  • Technician name, certification level and date, and the Level III review signature.

Readings that fall at or below the minimum are flagged to the owner's inspector right away so the decision does not wait for the final document.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Charleston

Charleston's climate shapes the plan. July highs average around 91 degrees Fahrenheit and the air is humid, so steel in the sun can be too hot for a standard probe and heat shimmer on tank shells affects coupling; early shifts help, and so do high-temperature probes. Winters are mild, with January highs near 59 degrees, so cold-weather limits rarely stop a job, but rain is frequent, especially from June through September, and wet couplant, wet surfaces and lightning delays need a contingency. Coastal moisture also means surfaces re-rust quickly after cleaning, so cleaning and scanning should happen in the same window.

Access matters as much as weather. Terminal and port facilities require badging and safety orientation, and some areas restrict personnel on active cargo operations. Industrial plants schedule outages, and Charleston area work often needs scaffolding or rope-free lift access that the owner must arrange. Atlantis does not keep an office in Charleston, so crews travel to your site, and lead time for mobilization should be built into the outage plan rather than assumed.

UT, MT or PT for your Charleston job

Pick the method for the damage you expect. Ultrasonic testing is the choice when the concern is internal: wall loss, laminations, weld volume. For surface cracks in carbon steel welds, such as crane and rigging components, magnetic particle inspection in Charleston is faster and more sensitive at the surface. Where the material is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, liquid penetrant testing in Charleston finds surface-breaking cracks. Many Charleston scopes use two of them together: UT thickness mapping of a pipe or vessel, with MT or PT on the weld repair that follows. The national pages for ultrasonic testing and the guide to ultrasonic testing explain the method further, and the Article 5 thickness measurement requirements write-up covers the code side.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Charleston employers with their own inspection staff often prefer to build the skill in house. The UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training courses cover theory, the practical technique and the documentation, and the ultrasonic simulator lets trainees practice scanning without wasting hours on a test block. Hands-on practice and examination take place at the employer's site under the employer's written practice, because under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel. See the North Charleston training page for how courses are delivered in the area.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cover in Charleston?
faq.a: It covers thickness surveys on tanks, piping, vessels and structural steel, and angle-beam examination of welds. Technicians travel to your Charleston site, work to your procedure or ours, and report each reading against the code that applies to the component.

faq.q: Can UT find corrosion under insulation or coating?
faq.a: Ultrasonic thickness readings can be taken through coatings when the instrument is set up for it, and through insulation once a window is cut. It measures remaining wall at the spot probed, so the survey plan decides how much corrosion gets found.

faq.q: Is UT accepted instead of radiography on welds?
faq.a: Some codes allow ultrasonic examination of production welds in place of radiography, including ASME B31.3 and AWS D1.1, and ASME Section VIII under conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree on the substitution before work starts.

faq.q: What surface condition does a thickness survey need?
faq.a: The surface should be free of loose scale, heavy rust, blistered paint and dirt so the probe couples properly. Light coating is often acceptable. Pitted or very rough areas may need grinding or wire brushing at each reading point before measurement.

faq.q: How do you measure hot piping or equipment?
faq.a: A high-temperature dual-element probe and couplant rated for the surface temperature are used, and the readings are corrected for the temperature of the wall. Keep contact times short and follow the safety limits set by the plant.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Charleston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charleston. Qualified technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and the report is reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III before it is issued to you.

faq.q: Who decides whether a thin reading is acceptable?
faq.a: For equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, your authorized inspector makes that decision. We supply the measured data and flag any reading at or below the stated minimum so you can act on it quickly.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic testing on aluminum and stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. Sound travels through both, but coarse grain in castings and austenitic welds attenuates the beam, so the technique, probe frequency and calibration block must suit the material. Tell us the alloy and thickness when you request a quote.

faq.q: How can my company get its own staff qualified in UT?
faq.a: Enroll technicians in Level 1 or Level 2 training, practice on the simulator, then complete hands-on practice and examination at your facility under your written practice. The employer, not the course provider, certifies the technician under SNT-TC-1A.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Charleston, SC | MT, MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Charleston, SC for crane welds, repaired steel, structural connections and forgings, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Charleston, South Carolina
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection in Charleston, South Carolina, checking carbon and low-alloy steel for surface and slightly subsurface cracks. Typical scopes are crane and lifting structures at the port, welds on repaired steel, structural connections, shafts and forgings. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and we reply within one business day when you submit the part list through the MT inspection quote form.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Charleston

Cracks start where steel is loaded repeatedly, and Charleston has a lot of repeatedly loaded steel. Container terminals on the Wando and Cooper Rivers lift boxes all day with ship-to-shore cranes, straddle carriers and yard equipment. Rail serves the terminals and the inland ports, so couplers, bogie frames and lifting lugs show up in repair shops. Manufacturing around North Charleston adds turbocharger housings, vehicle chassis components, fabricated frames and aircraft ground-support equipment. Bridges and elevated roadways such as the cable-stayed Cooper River crossing add structural connections that state engineers inspect on a schedule.

  • Cranes and rigging: hook blocks, shackles, padeyes, boom and girder welds, wire rope sockets and spreader frames.
  • Repair welding: weld toes and root-repair areas after cracks have been ground out, which is when MT proves the crack is gone.
  • Process and power plants: nozzle welds, support lugs, trunnions and attachment welds on vessels and boilers.
  • Machinery: shafts, gears, couplings, bolting and forgings that carry cyclic load.

What magnetic particle testing finds and what it misses

MT works only on ferromagnetic material, which in practice means carbon steel, low-alloy steel and most martensitic grades. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium, and a part made of those needs a different surface method. When the part is magnetized, a crack that cuts across the field lines leaks flux at the surface, and iron particles dusted or sprayed on the surface gather there to draw the crack. Surface-breaking flaws give the sharpest indications. Slightly subsurface flaws can show on clean, smooth parts, but the sensitivity falls quickly with depth.

MT does not size depth, and it does not see flaws buried deep in thick sections; that job belongs to ultrasonic testing. Heavy paint, scale and weld spatter hide fine cracks, so surface condition drives the result. Direction matters too: a crack parallel to the field lines produces little or no indication, which is why every area is examined twice with the field rotated roughly ninety degrees.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 7 sets how the examination is done: equipment, particles, field strength, lighting and documentation. Acceptance comes from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 puts MT methods and acceptance in Mandatory Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 addresses magnetic particle examination at paragraph 344.3 with acceptance limits in Table 341.3.2, and AWS D1.1 and D1.5 set acceptance for welded structures and bridges. Specifications usually cite ASTM E1444 as the practice, with ASTM E709 as the background guide. For cranes and rigging, owner and manufacturer specifications often drive the acceptance limits.

In South Carolina, boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act administered by the state's Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, which commonly requires MT or PT on weld repair areas, so the work we do on a repaired nozzle or attachment weld in the Charleston area usually feeds directly into a repair record. For in-service equipment, the owner's authorized inspector under API 510, 570 or 653 accepts or rejects the repair and decides what happens next.

Technique: yokes, prods, wet and dry particles

On site work in Charleston is usually done with a handheld electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the lifting test is repeated on a schedule. The yoke poles straddle the weld, the surface is dusted with dry colored powder or sprayed with a wet suspension, and any crack shows as a tight line of collected particles. The yoke is then turned about ninety degrees and the area examined again.

Prods inject current into the part and can reach awkward geometry, but they leave arc burns if poor contact is made, so many specifications restrict them. Visible particles on a contrast paint suit most field work. Wet fluorescent particles are more sensitive and are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which makes them useful on machined parts, shafts and bolting, and on critical welds when the owner calls for them. Residual magnetism is checked at the end, and parts are demagnetized when leftover fields would interfere with welding, machining or service.

Common findings on Charleston steel

The same few defects turn up repeatedly. On crane and lifting equipment the usual finding is fatigue cracking at weld toes, sharp section changes and bolt holes, where stress concentrates and repeated lifts open a crack over months or years. On repaired structures the finding is often an incomplete crack removal: the repair was welded over the tip of the original crack, and MT after grinding shows a trace of the old crack still present. In fabricated frames the typical findings are toe cracks, crater cracks at weld ends and hydrogen cracking in heavier sections that cooled too quickly.

Not every indication is a defect. Magnetic writing from contact with other steel, particles trapped at a sharp change in geometry and leakage at the boundary between weld metal and base metal can all mimic cracks. A competent technician recognizes them, cleans and re-examines the area, and records only what survives the second look. Where an indication is real but of unknown depth, the owner can follow up with ultrasonic examination or controlled grinding.

Who performs the work

Magnetic particle work is done by technicians qualified by Atlantis under its written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the test and interprets the indications, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the final report. The procedure names the code, the particle type, the lighting level and the evaluation criteria, so what the technician does in Charleston matches what the specification requires. If your procedure needs an independent review, the Level III consulting page explains that service.

Examination volume and sampling

Crane and lifting steel in a busy terminal is examined on a schedule, and the same marked areas are checked each time so that a growing crack can be compared with the last record.

How much of a structure gets examined is a scope decision, and it is best settled before the crew mobilizes. Construction codes often set a percentage of welds for examination; in-service programs rely on risk, with high-stress welds, repaired areas and past findings examined first. For a crane, the owner or manufacturer may list the critical welds and the intervals. When a crack is found in a sampled weld, the usual practice is to expand the examination to adjacent welds of the same type, and the quote should state how that expansion will be agreed so that a Charleston project does not stall while paperwork is exchanged.

What the MT report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material, surface condition and examined areas.
  • Procedure number and revision, plus the code and acceptance criteria applied.
  • Magnetizing method, current type, yoke lifting test result, particle type and carrier, and light levels where fluorescent particles are used.
  • Every relevant indication with location, length and orientation, recorded by sketch or photograph, with an accept or reject decision.
  • Whether demagnetization was performed and the residual field result.
  • Technician name and level, examination date and the Level III review.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Charleston

Humidity and salt are the Charleston factors. Wet suspensions work well in humid air, but dry powder clumps in damp conditions and surfaces flash-rust within hours of grinding, so surface preparation and examination should be scheduled together. Summer heat can raise steel temperatures beyond what the particles and contrast paint tolerate; the procedure should state a temperature limit, and shaded or early shifts avoid the problem. Winters are mild and rarely cause delays. Fluorescent work outdoors needs a tent or dark enclosure because Charleston sun overwhelms UV-A light.

Port terminals and industrial plants require badging, safety orientation and sometimes escorts. Crane inspections depend on equipment downtime, so the lead time for mobilization and access should be arranged early. Atlantis has no office in Charleston; crews travel to your site from elsewhere, and the plan should include their arrival and any hot-work or fall-protection requirements the site sets. Crane booms and elevated lifting equipment also call for an access platform, so confirm that before the crew travels.

MT, PT or UT for your Charleston job

For surface cracks in carbon steel, MT is the fastest and most sensitive field method. When the material is stainless steel or aluminum, use dye penetrant inspection in Charleston instead. When you need to know how deep a crack runs, or whether a weld has internal flaws, use ultrasonic inspection in Charleston. The national page on magnetic particle testing, the MT versus PT comparison and the Article 7 explainer go into more detail on choosing and on what the code requires.

Training your own magnetic particle technicians

If your Charleston operation inspects its own cranes or weld repairs, a trained in-house technician saves repeat mobilization. The MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training courses build the theory and the practical skills, and the NDT practice tests help trainees prepare. Qualification is completed at your facility under your written practice; check the SNT-TC-1A eligibility page for the experience hours employers typically require, and the North Charleston training page for the local delivery arrangements.

faq.q: Which Charleston equipment is a good fit for magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Carbon and low-alloy steel parts that see cyclic load: crane hooks and booms, shackles, lifting lugs, repaired welds, shafts and forgings. Stainless steel and aluminum parts cannot be examined by MT and should be checked with penetrant instead.

faq.q: Can MT be done through paint?
faq.a: A thin, uniform, tightly bonded coating is sometimes acceptable if the procedure was qualified for it, but heavy or flaking paint hides fine cracks. Most codes expect bare metal or a thin contrast coat, so plan to strip paint at the examination areas.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet fluorescent and dry visible MT?
faq.a: Dry or wet visible particles show against a contrast paint in normal light and suit most field work. Fluorescent particles are more sensitive and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which makes them better for fine cracks on critical parts.

faq.q: Why is the part magnetized in two directions?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it crosses the magnetic field at a steep angle. A crack aligned with the field gives almost no signal, so the area is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees to catch cracks in any direction.

faq.q: Does the part need demagnetizing afterward?
faq.a: Often yes. Residual magnetism can disturb arc welding, attract chips during machining, or interfere with instruments in service. The procedure states when demagnetization is required and the technician checks the residual field with a gauss meter.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Charleston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charleston. Technicians are mobilized to your port, plant or yard for the agreed scope, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews the report before it is issued.

faq.q: What should we prepare before the technician arrives?
faq.a: Clear access to every area to be examined, remove loose paint, scale and weld spatter, and tell us the material and any temperature limits. Provide a drawing or part list, the governing code and any site entry, safety or badging requirements.

faq.q: Can you examine welds on pressure vessels and piping?
faq.a: Yes, provided the weld is ferromagnetic. We examine to the method in ASME Section V Article 7 and report against the acceptance criteria of the governing code, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 or ASME B31.3.

faq.q: How hot can a part be for magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Wet particles and most contrast paints have temperature limits, and the procedure must state them. Hot parts can be examined only within the qualified range, so let the part cool or use a procedure qualified for the higher temperature.

faq.q: How can my Charleston staff learn magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Enroll them in MT Level 1 and Level 2 training, then complete practical training and examination at your site under your written practice. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies the technician, so your Level III should approve the practical examination.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Charleston, SC
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Charleston, SC for stainless, aluminum and steel welds, vessels, piping and machined parts, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Charleston, South Carolina
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, in Charleston, South Carolina. It finds surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium and carbon steel, and it suits the corrosion-resistant welds common in food, chemical and marine work. Technicians are mobilized to your site; request a quote through the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Charleston

Penetrant testing is the method for metals that magnets cannot handle, and the Charleston area has many of them. Port-side and marine fabrication uses aluminum and stainless steel. Food, beverage and chemical plants rely on stainless tanks, heat exchangers and sanitary piping whose welds must be crack-free. Aerospace and automotive suppliers around North Charleston machine aluminum, titanium and nickel alloy parts, and power and paper-mill piping includes stainless and alloy steels in corrosive service. PT also gets used on carbon steel welds where fluorescent or dye indications are easier to read than magnetic particle on complex shapes.

  • Stainless and alloy piping: root and cap passes, branch connections and socket welds in corrosive or sanitary service.
  • Vessels and exchangers: nozzle welds, tube-to-tubesheet welds, clad surfaces and repair excavations.
  • Marine aluminum: deck fittings, hull plate welds, handrail and equipment mounts exposed to salt water.
  • Machined and cast parts: housings, impellers, valve bodies and turbine components checked for surface cracks and porosity.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

PT finds only discontinuities that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid enters a crack by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the liquid back out so the crack appears as a bright line or spot. Anything buried below the surface is invisible, which means PT cannot see lack of fusion inside a weld or wall loss behind a surface. It works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

The weakness of the method is the surface. Cracks that are smeared closed by grinding, shot blasting or machining, cracks filled with paint, oil, scale or weld flux, and cracks in porous surfaces will not take up penetrant. Heavy surface roughness gives background that hides fine indications. Because of that, cleaning is part of the examination, and pre-cleaning, drying time and the choice of penetrant sensitivity decide whether the test is valid.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 describes the process and its controls, and ASTM E165 is the practice used for general industry work. ASME Section VIII Division 1 puts penetrant methods and acceptance in Mandatory Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 covers liquid penetrant examination at paragraph 344.4 with acceptance in Table 341.3.2, and AWS D1.1, D1.5 and D1.6 apply to welded structures, bridges and stainless fabrication. Where a specification names sensitivity levels or a penetrant family, the procedure follows it exactly.

Material controls matter for stainless and nickel alloys: the consumables are required to have low halogen and low sulfur content so they do not attack the metal, and the lot certificates are kept with the job file. For equipment inside South Carolina's boiler and pressure vessel regime, repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code under the oversight of the state Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, and PT of repair excavations and welds is a common requirement. On in-service equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector accepts or rejects the findings.

Technique: from cleaning to evaluation

The job begins with cleaning: mechanical removal of scale and spatter, then solvent cleaning to remove oil and residue. The surface is allowed to dry. A visible-dye or fluorescent penetrant is applied by spray or brush and left to dwell for the time stated in the procedure, which is set by material and expected defect type. Excess penetrant is removed according to the system in use: solvent removable, water washable or post-emulsifiable. A thin, even layer of developer is applied, and indications are evaluated after the developing time. Fluorescent penetrants are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened enclosure, and visible dye is read in good white light.

Temperature has direct effects. The standard range for both part and materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature using a comparator. Light colored dye on a cool, dry weld gives sharp indications, while a hot surface evaporates the penetrant before it works.

Choosing a penetrant system

Penetrant materials are grouped into families, and the choice affects sensitivity, cleanup and cost of the job. Visible dye penetrants are used in normal light and are the usual field choice for weld inspection on process piping. Fluorescent penetrants are brighter and reveal finer cracks, and are common for machined parts and critical welds. Each can be removed with solvent, with water, or by adding an emulsifier before washing, and each system has its own tolerances for the time penetrant sits on the surface.

Solvent-removable systems are the practical option for field work in Charleston because they need no water supply and leave little waste. Water-washable systems are faster on large or rough parts but need drains and a controlled rinse, which most outdoor sites cannot provide. The specification may fix the system; where it does not, the procedure selects it based on surface roughness, expected defect size and site conditions, and the report names the exact materials and lot numbers used.

Common findings with penetrant testing

On welds, penetrant most often reveals crater cracks, toe cracks, surface porosity and incomplete fusion at the weld surface. On castings and machined parts, it shows shrinkage cracks, laps, seams and grinding cracks. In service, it finds fatigue cracks, stress corrosion cracking in stainless equipment, and cracks started at weld repairs. Tight stress corrosion cracks can be difficult to see because they close up under residual stress, so surface preparation by light etching or careful cleaning matters more on these parts.

False indications are also common. Rough surfaces, scratches, weld spatter and incomplete removal of excess penetrant produce red or glowing patches that look like flaws. The technician wipes the area, re-applies developer and looks again; real cracks bleed back, while false indications fade or move. Only indications that persist are measured and recorded.

Who performs the work

PT is carried out by technicians qualified by the company under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician controls the process steps, performs the test and evaluates what is found; an ASNT NDT Level III writes and approves the procedure and signs off the report. Procedures for Charleston work name the penetrant system, the dwell times, the temperature range and the acceptance code. If your own procedures need review or you want a written practice drafted, the written practice development service is available.

Process records that keep results defensible

Charleston's humid air makes records especially important, since the conditions on the day affect the result.

A penetrant result is only as good as the record of how it was obtained. Weld repair excavations are examined before rewelding and again afterward, and each result is traceable to a procedure, a material lot and a technician. Where a customer or authorized inspector watches the work, they can verify the dwell and development times directly. Where they do not, the record has to show them. That is why the checklist of steps is completed on site rather than reconstructed later, and why photographs of indications are taken before the developer dries or fades.

What the PT report contains

  • Component or weld identification and material, and the areas examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, code, acceptance criteria and sensitivity level.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer brand and lot numbers, including the halogen and sulfur certificates on stainless and nickel alloy jobs.
  • Surface temperature, pre-clean method, dwell time and development time.
  • Each relevant indication with location, size and type (linear or rounded), recorded by sketch or photo, with the accept or reject call.
  • Technician name and level, date and the Level III review.

Planning a penetrant job in Charleston

The Charleston climate helps and hurts. Mild winters keep most mornings within the 40 to 125 degree window, but July highs near 91 degrees mean steel in the sun can pass the upper limit, so examining in shade or at dawn avoids a procedure requalification. Humidity slows drying after cleaning and can leave moisture in tight cracks that blocks penetrant, so plan time for drying. Rain and wind are real issues outdoors: tenting the area protects both the surface and the technician's view of the indications. Coastal salt contamination on stainless surfaces should be washed off before testing, because chlorides also affect the metal.

Plant sites need badging and permits for solvent use and hot surfaces, and port terminals restrict access. Atlantis has no office in Charleston, so technicians travel to your site; the plan should cover lodging, safety orientation and chemical handling approvals.

PT, MT or UT for your Charleston job

Choose penetrant for non-magnetic metals and for surface cracks on complex shapes. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Charleston for carbon steel when speed and sensitivity at the surface matter, and ultrasonic testing in Charleston when you need to look inside the wall or weld. The national page for penetrant testing and the Article 6 requirements explained give more depth, and the MT versus PT guide compares the two surface methods side by side.

Training your own penetrant technicians

Penetrant testing is a quick method to learn well, and many Charleston manufacturers train their own staff. The PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training courses cover the process and the code requirements, and the penetrant testing simulator gives trainees repetition on process steps. Employers finish qualification on site under their written practice, and the North Charleston training page explains how courses are arranged for the Charleston area.

faq.q: Which materials can be inspected with liquid penetrant?
faq.a: Any non-porous material: stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, copper alloys and carbon steel. PT detects only flaws open to the surface, so it does not replace ultrasonic testing for internal weld defects.

faq.q: How do dye penetrant and fluorescent penetrant differ?
faq.a: Visible dye is read in white light and is simple for field use. Fluorescent penetrant is read under UV-A light in a dark enclosure and is more sensitive to tight cracks, so specifications for critical parts often call for it.

faq.q: Why does surface cleaning matter so much?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale and flux fill cracks and keep penetrant out, and smeared metal from grinding closes them. A flaw that penetrant cannot enter cannot be found, so cleaning and drying are treated as part of the examination.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 allows 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, so we plan shade, enclosures or schedule changes for hot Charleston days.

faq.q: Why are halogen and sulfur limits used on stainless steel?
faq.a: Chlorides, fluorides and sulfur can attack stainless and nickel alloys during later service or heating. Low-contaminant penetrant materials are used on these metals, and the lot certificates are kept in the job record.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Charleston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Charleston. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews each report before it goes to you.

faq.q: What happens if an indication is doubtful?
faq.a: The area is wiped, cleaned and developed again to see whether the indication returns. Real cracks bleed back in the same place; false indications from roughness or leftover penetrant fade. The technician records only indications that persist, and your inspector decides what to do next.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks under a weld surface?
faq.a: No. Penetrant only shows discontinuities that break the surface. Buried lack of fusion, slag or porosity needs ultrasonic testing, and carbon steel cracks just below the surface may show with magnetic particle.

faq.q: How do you evaluate indications from penetrant testing?
faq.a: Each indication is measured, classified as linear or rounded, and compared with the acceptance table in the governing code. Doubtful indications are wiped clean and re-developed to confirm whether they are real or false.

faq.q: How can Charleston employers train penetrant technicians?
faq.a: Enroll them in PT Level 1 and Level 2 training, use the simulator for repetition, then complete practical examination at your facility under your written practice. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, with your Level III approving the process.
